newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo stocks manage mild bounce but gloom lingers.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo stocks manage mild bounce but gloom lingers.

text.p: Tokyo stocks bounced back from a three-day losing streak on Friday, invigorated by a Wall Street rally, but trade was volatile and brokers said the turnaround could be shortlived.

The economic worries that sent stocks spiralling to their lowest close in a year on Thursday were still hanging over the market and Tokyo's key index struggled to stay in positive territory, despite the strong U.S. stocks.
Brokers said the overall direction was still downward due to widespread unease about the prospects for Japan's already anaemic economic recovery.

The stock market's benchmark Nikkei average of 225 leading shares closed up 0.61 percent, or 119.79 points at 19,690.46 after an indecisive session in which the index see-sawed between losses and gains.

On Thursday, the Nikkei fell a steep 2.6 percent to 19,570.67, its lowest close since last December, as the market fretted about the uncertain strength of the Japanese economy and the outlook for corporate profits.
Brokers said that Friday's rebound was fairly feeble, with the surge on Wall Street tipping the balance.

"The Nikkei 225 posted a mild recovery today just because of the New York rally, but I still expect it to head downwards next week or in January," said Haruyoshi Mabuchi, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center.

The market has been dismayed this week by confirmation that the government plans to scrap special tax cuts that had previously been granted to help the economy recover. This will be on top of an unpopular rise in the consumption tax from three to five percent due next April as the government tries to bring a big budget deficit under control.
Although financial policymakers proclaim on a regular basis that the recovery is picking up steam and will continue into next year, scepticism persists.
"The government decided to end special income tax cuts and to raise the consumption tax. This made us worry about whether the government is really trying to support the economy," Mabuchi said.
Japan's economic recovery has been slow to gear up, despite record low interest rates and government public works spending.

"We understand that the government needs to balance its budget. But at the same time, the market wants to see specific deregulatory measures to prop up the economy," said Tetsuya Ishijima, chief strategist at Okasan Securities Co Ltd.
Analysts say doubts about whether authorities can pull off the planned "Big Bang" reform plan to revitalise Tokyo's flagging markets are also adding to the despondency.

On Thursday in New York, the Dow ended up 126.87 points, or two percent, at 6,473.64, its second biggest points gain on record. The rise was spurred by a powerful bond market rally and a flurry of options-related buying.
